questions.question: Calculate the four operating-cycle indicators for Ngcobo and Venter Traders and interpret them together as one story.
questions.expected_answer: Stock turnover rate: cost of sales R1 800 000 over average stock of R225 000 — opening R232 500 and closing R217 500 — gives 8 times a year. Stock holding period: average stock over cost of sales times 365 gives 45,6 days per refill — the same fact as the rate, expressed in days. Debtors' collection period: average debtors R61 000 over credit sales of R1 440 000, times 365, gives 15,5 days — strong against 30-day terms. Creditors' payment period: average creditors R93 000 over credit purchases of R1 356 000, times 365, gives 25 days. Read together: money is locked in stock about 46 days and in debtors about 15 — roughly 61 days from buying stock to banking the cash — while suppliers are paid at day 25, so the gap is financed from the business's own pocket. Collections are excellent; the six-and-a-half-week shelf suits a paint and tile trade but deserves watching; and paying at 25 days on 30-day terms surrenders about five days of free credit unless an early-settlement discount is earned in exchange.

questions.question: Calculate the debt-equity ratio and the return on average partners' equity, and give a full comment on each, including the case for or against more borrowing.
questions.expected_answer: Debt-equity: non-current liabilities R185 000 to equity R889 800 gives 0,2 to 1 — for every rand of the partners' money, outsiders hold about twenty cents of long-term money. This is low gearing: safe, with light exposure to interest rates. But because the business earns far more on its funds than the loan's 12 percent cost, a case exists for gearing up carefully to expand — borrowing earns its keep whenever the return on the borrowed rand exceeds its cost. Return on average partners' equity: net profit R528 000 over average equity R846 300 — opening R802 800 and closing R889 800 — gives 62,4 percent. Compared with roughly 8 to 10 percent risk-free in a fixed deposit, the return is outstanding; the comment must concede that the partners' own labour sits inside the figure, since their salaries are appropriations rather than expenses, yet even after mentally pricing that labour the investment comfortably beats the alternative. Solvency confirms the safety: total assets to total liabilities is R1 175 400 to R285 600, or 4,1 to 1.

questions.question: Write a four-part comment on the liquidity of the business, and explain why an indicator must never be judged on its own.
questions.expected_answer: Figure and comparison: the current ratio is 4,2 to 1 — current assets R420 400 to current liabilities R100 600 — and the acid-test is 2,0 to 1, both comfortably above the traditional comfort levels of about 2 to 1 and 1 to 1. Direction: liquidity is very strong — short-term debts are covered even if no further stock is sold. Cause: fast debtor collections at 15,5 days and a large bank balance of over R134 000 keep liquid assets high. Consequence and advice: no payday can embarrass the business, but it is over-liquid — idle cash earns next to nothing — so the partners should put surplus funds to work: expansion, reducing the 12 percent loan, or earning early-settlement discounts. Indicators must be read in pairs because one number can carry two stories: a climbing current ratio can mean strengthening liquidity or unsold stock silting up, and only the stock holding period says which; likewise a turnover rate rising and a holding period falling are the identical news in two languages. Every figure needs its comparison — last year, the norm, the policy — before it means anything at all.
